title: 5 Habits That Get Senior Experts Taken Seriously Without Raising Their Voice
author: Is Public Speaking
summary: The piece argues that professional deference is inferred by colleagues from small observable behaviors, not granted in response to stated credentials -- and that quieter people, not louder ones, often earn the most standing. It identifies the core mistake as 'asking for' respect by citing years of experience or past achievements, which the author says signals the opposite of authority because it treats the question of one's standing as still open. The centerpiece technique is a two-second pause before answering any consequential question, even ones the speaker already knows cold, on the theory that instant answers read as reflexes while a brief pause reads as considered judgment and quietly transfers conversational tempo to the speaker. The author also frames the pause as protective, since most regretted remarks are made in the first second after being challenged. The post ends by previewing four further behavioral 'signals' -- holding a sentence so a room stops talking over it, ending an interruption without words, responding to a competitor's success, and calling out bad behavior in a way that builds rather than costs standing.
points: The core claim: deference is inferred from observed behavior (how you handle time, words, and disagreement), not granted in response to stated credentials -- citing your years of experience signals the question of your standing is still open.

The signature technique is a deliberate two-second pause before answering, applied especially to questions the speaker already knows the answer to, so instant answers don't get discounted as mere reflex.

The pause is framed as doing double duty: it reads externally as considered judgment while also giving the speaker a buffer against saying something regrettable in the first second after being challenged.
The author explicitly distinguishes this approach from volume or dominance, noting the most respected person in their prior company was 'not the loudest one... and was not the most senior either.'
quotes: The most respected person in my last company was not the loudest one, and she was not the most senior either.

I spent a long time assuming this was a confidence problem, and that fixing it meant becoming someone louder. That turned out to be wrong twice over. The people who got deference in my last company were not louder, and several of them were markedly quieter than the people who did not.
Deference is inferred rather than granted. People work it out from how you handle your time, your words, and your disagreements, and they do it fast.

Speed reads as reaction. When you answer instantly, the room infers the answer was available without thought, which is fine for facts and damaging for judgment. A pause implies the question was worth considering, and by extension that you are the kind of person who considers things.
Most of the things you regret saying arrived in the first second after a challenge. The gap is where you catch them, which means the same habit that builds standing also stops you damaging it.

Do it especially when you already know the answer. This is the counterintuitive part. Answering instantly on the questions you know cold trains the room to read your instant answers as reflexes, which devalues the ones that took work.
